frameworks.name: Past-Behavior Structured Interviewing (STAR)
frameworks.citation: Campion, M. A., Pursell, E. D., & Brown, B. K. (1988). Structured interviewing: Raising the psychometric properties of the employment interview. Personnel Psychology, 41(1), 25-42.
frameworks.rationale: Structured behavioral questions raise interview reliability and predictive validity from r ≈ .14 (unstructured) to r ≈ .56.

frameworks.name: Structured Interview Meta-Analysis
frameworks.citation: Levashina, J., Hartwell, C. J., Morgeson, F. P., & Campion, M. A. (2014). The structured employment interview: Narrative and quantitative review of the research literature. Personnel Psychology, 67(1), 241-293.
frameworks.rationale: Confirms that structure — not narrative polish — produces validity, and that anchored content-based rating scales outperform global impression ratings.

frameworks.name: Neurodiversity-Affirming Adaptations
frameworks.citation: Maras, K., Norris, J. E., Nicholson, J., Heasman, B., Remington, A., & Crane, L. (2021). Ameliorating the disadvantage for autistic job seekers: An initial evaluation of adapted employment interview questions. Autism, 25(4), 1060-1075.
frameworks.rationale: Tested explicit, multi-part, literal-friendly question formats with autistic candidates and found that adaptations to question wording and scoring expectations — not changes in candidate ability — closed most of the rating gap. Justifies rewarding clarification, literal answers, and concrete factual specificity over storytelling polish.

frameworks.name: Practitioner guidance
frameworks.citation: AskEARN — Including Neurodivergent Workers: Job Descriptions and Interviewing.
frameworks.rationale: U.S. DOL-funded Employer Assistance and Resource Network on Disability Inclusion.

0.label: Ignores ambiguity
0.criteria: Ignores ambiguity; answers a question that wasn't asked.

1.label: Notices but proceeds
1.criteria: Notices vagueness but proceeds without resolving it.
1.example: I guess you mean at work — I'll go with that.

2.label: Asks clarifying or states interpretation
2.criteria: Asks a focused clarifying question, OR explicitly states the interpretation being used.
2.example: Do you mean a conflict with a coworker or with a customer? I'll answer the coworker case.

0.label: Single blob
0.criteria: Single undifferentiated blob; missing 3+ STAR elements.

1.label: 2 of 4 STAR elements
1.criteria: Covers 2 of 4 STAR elements (e.g., Situation + Action only).

2.label: All 4 elements
2.criteria: Covers all four — Situation, Task, Action, Result — in any order. Bullet-style, list-style, or chronological all count equally.

dimensions.name: Specificity (concrete > general)
dimensions.framework_source: Maras 2020 (provide examples, give details); Levashina 2014 (content-based scales)

0.label: Generalities only
0.example: I'm a team player and I always communicate well.

1.label: Mixed
1.criteria: Mixes one concrete detail with generalities.

2.label: Concrete factual
2.criteria: Names a specific event, role, action, tool, or number. Literal/factual phrasing scores fully here.
2.example: In March 2024, on the QA team, I rewrote the test plan and cut regression time from 4h to 90min.

0.label: Doesn't match or no outcome
0.criteria: Example doesn't match the question, or no outcome given.

1.label: Loose match
1.criteria: Example matches loosely; outcome implied but not stated.

2.label: Match + outcome
2.criteria: Example clearly matches what was asked AND states an outcome (what happened, what was learned, or what changed). A null/negative outcome honestly reported scores fully.

worked_examples.prompt: Tell me about a time you handled a conflict at work.

strong.label: S1 — literal / low-flair
strong.response: Situation: A teammate and I disagreed on the database schema in May 2024. Task: Pick one design before sprint end. Action: I wrote a one-page comparison doc with three trade-offs and we reviewed it together. Result: We picked their option with two of my changes. Sprint shipped on time.
strong.reasoning: Hits all four STAR elements explicitly (D2 = 2), highly specific (D3 = 2), outcome stated (D4 = 2). No narrative arc required. Note D1 = 2 because by labeling each STAR element the candidate is explicitly stating their interpretation.

strong.label: S2 — asks clarifying question first
strong.response: Quick clarification — do you mean conflict over a decision or interpersonal conflict? … OK, decision conflict. Last quarter, our designer and I disagreed on the onboarding flow. I proposed running a 5-user test; we did, the data favored her version, we shipped it, retention rose 6%.
strong.reasoning: Models D1 = 2 (clarification rewarded, not penalized), then full STAR.

strong.label: S3 — conventional narrative
strong.response: At my last job a coworker missed deadlines repeatedly. I scheduled a 1:1, asked what was blocking him, found out he had no access to the staging server, got him access the same day, and the next two sprints he hit every deadline.
strong.reasoning: Strong specificity and outcome; Task is implied rather than stated (D2 = 1).

weak.label: W1 — generalities
weak.response: I think communication is really key. I always try to listen and find common ground because conflict is just part of any workplace.
weak.reasoning: No event, no STAR, no outcome.

weak.label: W2 — wrong question
weak.response: I love working in teams. One time my team won an award for collaboration — it was amazing.

weak.label: W3 — story with no result
weak.response: There was this whole thing with a coworker, it was tense, we had a meeting, then another meeting, things were said. Anyway, that's what happened.
weak.reasoning: Narrative-ish but no concrete actions, no outcome (D3 = 1, D4 = 0). Demonstrates that 'story flow' alone earns nothing.

do_not_score: Narrative polish, story arc, or engaging delivery
Emotional expressiveness, warmth, charisma, executive presence
Small talk, rapport-building openers, tone-matching the interviewer
Eye-contact references, body-language descriptions, vocal variety
Verbosity or word count — a 60-word literal answer can score 8/8
Hedging language vs. confident language ('I think…' vs. 'I did…') — score the content, not the register
Disclosure or non-disclosure of neurodivergence — both are valid; score neither up nor down
Use of 'I' vs. 'we' — score whether the action is concrete, not the pronoun
Asking a clarifying question — this is rewarded in D1, never penalized as not knowing the answer
Pauses, 'let me think', or requesting to re-read the prompt
evaluator_directive: None of the do_not_score items correlate with structured-interview validity (Levashina et al., 2014), and several actively penalize autistic communication styles (Maras et al., 2020). If you find yourself wanting to deduct for any of them, re-score on content only.
attribution: Interview response rubric grounded in past-behavior structured interviewing (Campion, Pursell, & Brown, 1988; Levashina, Hartwell, Morgeson, & Campion, 2014) with neurodiversity-affirming adaptations from Maras et al. (2021, Autism).
